metadata.title: Holder v. Hall, 512 U.S. 874 (1994) (No. 91-2012)
metadata.creator: Supreme Court of the United States
metadata.description:
Case name: Holder v. Hall

Opinion filed: 1994-06-30

Docket No.: 91-2012

Citations:
• 129 L. Ed. 2d 687
• 114 S. Ct. 2581
• 512 U.S. 874
• 1994 U.S. LEXIS 5083

Case holding summaries:
• "under Section 5 ... the proposed voting practice should be measured against the existing voting practice to determine whether retrogression would result from the proposed change...." The "baseline for comparison is present by definition; it is the existing status"
• “The baseline for comparison is present by definition; it is the existing status.”
• noting the solicitor general had reasoned (improperly), "the Hispanic legislators elected from Hispanic districts in Dade County would represent, not just the interests of the Dade County Hispanics, but the interests of all the Hispanics in the State" (citation omitted)
• “But ‘we have never applied stare decisis mechanically to prohibit overruling our earlier decisions determining the meaning of statutes.’”
• noting the solicitor general had reasoned (improperly), "the Hispanic legislators elected from Hispanic districts in Dade County would represent, not just the interests of the Dade County Hispanics, but the interests of all the Hispanics in the State" (citation omitted)
• “This case presents the question whether the size of a governing authority is subject to a vote dilution challenge under § 2 of the Voting Rights Act”
• separate opinion of Stevens, J.
• legislative history "is read selectively to support the result the Court intends to achieve"
• holding that the size of a governing body is not subject to a Section 2 vote dilution challenge
• "But `we have never applied stare decisis mechanically to prohibit overruling our earlier decisions determining the meaning of statutes.'"
• separate opinion of Stevens, J.
• "The baseline for comparison is present by definition; it is the existing status."
• “Resort to legislative history is only justified where the face of the [statute] is inescap- ably ambiguous.”
• binding opinion of Kennedy, J.
• noting that "the power to influence the political process is not limited to winning elections"
• rejecting the "failure of [the minority group] to have legislative seats in proportion to its population" as a sufficient basis for a claim
• change from three-member commission to five-member commission is subject to § 5 preclearance
• rejecting a "single-member-office" exception to § 2
• "Again in 1975, both the House and Senate Judiciary Committees, in recommending extension of the Act, noted with approval the `broad interpretations to the scope of Section 5' in Allen and Perkins v. Matthews [400 U. S. 379 (1971)]"
• the Act must "be interpreted in light of its prophylactic purpose and the historical experience which it reflects"
• it "is not disputed" that an expansion in the size of a board of education is subject to § 5 preclearance
• noting that there is no decision of this Court holding a legislative apportionment plan violative of the Fifteenth Amendment
• in the 1982 extension of the Act, "Congress specifically endorsed a broad construction" of § 5
• "After extensive deliberations in 1970 on bills to extend the Voting Rights Act, during which the Allen case was repeatedly discussed, the Act was extended for five years, without any substantive modification of § 5"
• remand of challenge to solecommissioner system with instructions to consider size and geographic compactness within proposed three- and five-member commission forms of government
• change in size is a change in a "standard, practice, or procedure" because the change "increase[s] or diminish[es] the number of officials for whom the electorate may vote"
• concluding that it would be "anomalous" to do otherwise
• "Even if serious problems lie ahead in applying the `totality of the circumstances' [inquiry under § 2(b) of the Voting Rights Act], that task, difficult as it may prove to be, cannot justify a judicially created limitation on the coverage of the broadly worded statute[.]"
• declaring that the "single-member district is generally the appropriate standard against which to measure minority group potential to elect"
• "Under the ejusdem generis rule of construction the general words are confined to the class and may not be used to enlarge it"
• recognizing that systems that "classify and separate voters by race" threaten "to undermine our system of representative democracy by signaling to elected officials that they represent a particular racial group rather than their constituency as a whole"
• O'Connor, J., joined by Burger, C. J., and Powell and Rehnquist, JJ., concurring in judgment
• "There is no principled reason why one size [of an elected governing body] should be picked over another as the benchmark for [determining whether vote dilution exists]."
• separate opinion of Stevens, J.
